title: Findings from the $1M Vercel Sandbox challenge
summary:
In August, we launched the $1M hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox, inviting security researchers to try and escape Vercel Sandbox. We also coordinated with cybersecurity experts Trail of Bits to review the source code and security architecture.

Here is a summary of the challenge:

  • 1,285 reports over two weeks

  • $242,000 in bounties paid out

  • One Linux kernel zeroday vulnerability uncovered

No reports showed anyone accessing customer data in Vercel Sandbox. The most severe finding was the defect in the upstream Linux kernel.

The kernel zero day

The program's most important report arrived on day three.

Paulos Yibelo (pwn.ai), a HackerOne researcher working from a standard sandbox with no special access, found a defect in the Linux kernel's networking stack. Paulos discovered that specially crafted packets sent from within the microVM enabled three different attacks:

  1. Leak host memory over the network

  2. Crash the host machine

  3. Execute code on the host

Leaking host memory

In the first attack, memory from the host, the machine your sandbox shares with other tenants, shows up in packets the guest sends over the internet. This can happen continuously, for as long as the guest keeps sending.

This attack was demonstrated against Vercel production sandboxes.

Crashing the host and executing code on the host

The researcher also found that by sending specific packets, they could compromise the host.

First, by sending two packets, the researcher crashed the host machine, shutting down every sandbox running on it. Second, using the same flaw, they were able to run commands with full administrator privileges on the host, breaking out of the sandbox’s isolation boundary.

The packet-related crash and code execution attacks were demonstrated on the researcher’s own KVM and Firecracker machines matching Vercel Sandbox configuration.

Responsibly disclosing the kernel vulnerability

Almost every major cloud provider isolates customer workloads on this same layer of the Linux kernel, so any defect is shared-infrastructure risk.

Immediately after being notified, we collaborated with the researcher to understand and mitigate the vulnerability, working with AWS and other industry partners to prioritize a fix, and ensuring that Vercel customers and other developers using the kernel were safe.

The researcher also contacted the kernel maintainers and worked with them to create candidate patches. Fixes are under private review and CVEs are pending, so we are not publishing additional details until the patches are public. We are disclosing the existence of the vulnerability because it was separately disclosed in public.

Our approach to pressure-testing Vercel Sandbox

The HackerOne challenge made bounties available to any researcher, but we also extended our program to include internal evaluations and an independent investigation.

Before launching the public bounty, we performed live security assessments internally with full source access and support from the engineers who created and maintain Vercel Sandbox. We also engaged Trail of Bits, bringing on two engineers to evaluate our security architecture.

Not every finding came from the outside. Marcos Hernanz, a Vercel intern, found a cross-tenant data leak in the Linux device-mapper storage layer. This vulnerability let any sandbox read recycled disk blocks from previously deleted sandboxes.

The white-box deep dive

Trail of Bits spent four engineer-weeks inside our source code, with full access to the repositories and two enterprise test teams. They delivered 20 findings, and each was tested, confirmed, and referenced to the exact code.

They also performed an architectural review and concluded that our virtualization boundary is sound. Each sandbox runs on its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and the device model is deliberately tiny. No guest shares a running kernel with the host, or with another tenant.

On top of that foundation, they gave us three structural recommendations, which we implemented:

  • Find and eliminate all trust in the guest. Our control plane accepted values returned by software running inside the microVM, and every one of those values is tenant input. Anything that crosses the boundary should be derived server-side or signed with a key the guest cannot reach.

  • One policy, one decider. Egress enforcement was split across subsystems that each parsed the same network policy independently, and they did not always agree. We now use one canonicalization routine per data type, one component per decision, and revalidate connections when policy changes.

  • Assume the next zero day. We strengthened the protections around each sandbox to limit the damage if an attacker exploits the virtualization software. We keep host kernels up to date, have disabled nested virtualization, and use Firecracker’s jailer to run each microVM process with restricted permissions and isolate it from the rest of the host.

Vercel Sandbox findings

We received 1,285 reports in two weeks. This volume is only possible because researchers now hunt at AI speed.

Here is a breakdown of reports by category:

  • 877 duplicates

  • 319 not applicable

  • 57 valid

  • 32 informative

In our report triage we have validated:

  • 1 Critical finding

  • 5 High findings

  • 9 Medium findings

  • 42 Low findings

  • 32 Informative findings

We have paid out $242,000 in bug bounties.

The medium, Low, and Informative findings are small policy-boundary gaps, like a firewall rule that behaved differently than documented and a field that trusted the guest more than it should.

The most severe finding was the Linux kernel zero day defect, and no reports showed anyone reading a customer’s files, secrets, or application data.

We were most impressed with the heterogeneity of the reports. It was clear that researchers used different setups and have different obsessions. Some clearly know Linux namespaces and steered their agents straight at the kernel boundary. Others went after the network policies, and many went after areas we didn’t think to put on the menu.

That variety is what you're funding with a public challenge. Here's one of the more interesting findings it produced.

Cross-tenant disk snapshot restore (with limits)

Filed on day one of the challenge, this report is our favorite example of why we run a public bug bounty, even after internal assessments and a white-box engagement.

When you snapshot a sandbox, the control plane has to record where the snapshot data landed: {storage_url, size, checksum}. The flaw the researcher found was subtle: that answer came from software running inside the guest, and services running on the host trusted it. That is a trust-boundary violation. The guest is where our customers (and hackers) run untrusted code, so the host can never take its word as authoritative.

The researcher combined a known, documented container-escape primitive with this trust flaw. They intercepted the snapshot response inside their own sandbox and rewrote it, swapping the storage objects of two snapshots belonging to two separate accounts they owned. That meant restoring "your" snapshot materialized the other account's entire filesystem.

The researcher demonstrated that each account could read and modify the other’s files, verified the results using hashes, and preserved the test resources so we could independently reproduce the findings.

The limits of this attack matter. Aiming the swap at a specific victim required knowing that victim's internal snapshot storage key, a random 96-bit identifier the platform generates per snapshot and never exposes through the API. The only place that key appears is inside the victim's own sandbox. The researcher owned both accounts, which is what made the proof possible; there was no demonstrated path for a stranger to target another tenant. We still treated it as a priority fix, because a boundary that depends on a secret staying secret is not a boundary.

Trail of Bits independently flagged the same root cause in their assessment, which told us the finding was real, important, and discoverable from two completely different angles.

The fix shipped within a week, and the control plane now binds every snapshot object to the project that created it and rejects anything else. Snapshot creation moved out of the guest-reachable environment into a host-side service, and storage paths are project-scoped with strictly validated URLs.

Thank you to the research community

We would like to thank every researcher who filed a report, whether their finding was a zero day or a duplicate. Every technique discovered in the challenge informs how we protect the workloads running on Vercel Sandbox.

Thank you also to Trail of Bits for your comprehensive internal investigation and guidance.

Read the original challenge announcement and learn more about Vercel Sandbox in the documentation.

title: Amazon S3 joins the Vercel Marketplace
summary:
You can now create and connect Amazon S3 resources through the Vercel Marketplace without leaving your Vercel project dashboard.

The Amazon S3 Marketplace integration automatically adds connection details as environment variables and lets you manage resources alongside your application infrastructure, with links to AWS for deeper configuration. Authentication uses short-lived OIDC credentials without storing static AWS keys.

Amazon S3 is also available in v0, which provisions resources, configures connections, and generates code from your prompt.

Vercel Blob provides public and private storage for application file uploads, with built-in caching and CDN delivery close to your end users. Choose the Amazon S3 integration for existing AWS workflows, analytics on managed Iceberg tables with S3 Tables, or vector storage and search with S3 Vectors.

Get started in the Vercel Marketplace. Create a new AWS account through Vercel to receive $100 USD in credits, valid for six months, or link an existing account and manage your plan and usage from your Vercel dashboard. Linked accounts support only new buckets created through Vercel. Read the AWS announcement for examples and setup details.

title: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning now available on AI Gateway for free
summary:
Nemotron 3.5 Lightning from NVIDIA is now available for free on AI Gateway as nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-free, served by NVIDIA.

Nemotron 3.5 Lightning is an open-weight reasoning and chat model for long-running agents, sub-agent work, chatbots, and RAG systems. The model has 30B parameters with 3B active per token, in a hybrid Mixture-of-Experts design that interleaves Mamba-2 and MoE layers with a few attention layers. It has a 1M token context window and supports tool calling and structured outputs.

Note: The provider may retain prompts for model improvement.

Call Nemotron 3.5 Lightning through the AI SDK, the Chat Completions, Responses, and Messages APIs, or a coding agent connected to AI Gateway.

Use nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-free as the model name:

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Then select nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-free in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

title: Repository checkout and Git LFS downloads are now faster
summary:
Repository checkout and Git LFS downloads are now faster on Vercel, reducing the time spent preparing your project's files before a build.

During rollout on build machines with more than two vCPUs:

  • The average time to get project files ready fell by 20%.

  • For LFS-enabled projects, the average time to get project files ready fell by 54%, saving approximately 13 seconds per deployment on this step.

  • The 90th-percentile time to get project files ready fell by 22%. This means 90% of deployments finish this step in that time or less.

These improvements apply automatically, with no action required. Read the Git deployment documentation to learn more.

title: Gemini 4 Argon now available on AI Gateway
summary:
Gemini 4 Argon from Google is now available on AI Gateway.

Gemini 4 Argon is built for coding, agentic work, and complex reasoning. It has a 1M token context window, accepts text, image, PDF, and video input, and supports tool calling.

On coding tasks, Gemini 4 Argon builds features, fixes bugs, and researches unfamiliar codebases, carrying longer tasks through multiple steps. The model also reads dense diagrams, spreadsheets, layout-heavy documents, and video, which suits tasks like a financial analysis spread across several spreadsheet tabs. Beyond code, it handles work in finance, health, and law, and hard problems in math and science. Gemini 4 Argon uses thinking levels (low, medium, and high) instead of thinking budgets.

title: Muse Wonder now available on AI Gateway
summary:
Muse Wonder from Meta is now available on AI Gateway. The model is designed for coding, long-running agents, and computer use. It can plan multi-step tasks, delegate work to sub-agents, and recover from errors as work progresses.

Muse Wonder has a 1M-token context window and supports text, image, and PDF input, tool calling, and structured output. Agents can work with code, screenshots, and documents in the same workflow.

You can access the model through AI Gateway with one API key, without creating a separate Meta account.

Set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY in your environment, then use meta/muse-wonder-1.0 as the model name:

title: How Rillet ships 3× faster with AI agents on Vercel
summary:
Rillet on Vercel

  • Tripled shipping rate in three months with eve agents deployed on Vercel

  • Two-person team closed 800+ Linear tickets in its first 4 months

  • Builder access via Enterprise Managed Users, SSO, and Directory Sync

  • Ships customer-requested changes to production in as little as two hours

  • Gives every builder access to models through AI Gateway

Rillet is an AI-native enterprise resource planning (ERP) platform. Their AI agents do accounting work inside a real-time general ledger, with human approval and a full audit trail. Rillet serves more than 600 customers working toward a zero-day close, reducing the time needed to close their books at month-end.

A product that helps customers close their books in near real time needs a team that can respond quickly to their requests. Anthony Liang heads Rillet’s two-person frontend team, formed only a few months ago, and leads the push to put agents to work across internal workflows, from shipping customer fixes to reviewing code.

The team builds agents with eve and runs them on Vercel, using Vercel Connect to give them access to Slack and Linear, while AI Gateway routes their model requests.

Standardizing every internal agent on eve

Anthony had been building AI applications since the GPT-3.5 era and had evaluated nearly every agent framework on the market, from the major model providers' SDKs to the open-source ecosystem. Each gave him primitives for the model loop but left him to decide where instructions lived, how tools registered, and how an agent reached Slack and GitHub.

Anthony could make those choices for his own agents, but he wanted conventions everyone at Rillet could follow, including people who had never touched TypeScript.

An agent is a directory

Anthony chose eve, Vercel's open-source agent framework for building, running, and scaling agents that keeps instructions, tools, and skills together in one directory.

People who know what an agent should do can shape its behavior through markdown instructions and skills without writing code, while its tools live in TypeScript files whose names become the API. Once an agent is ready, it can move from a laptop to Vercel without changing how it behaves. Rillet manages all of these deployments in one company-controlled Vercel organization.

Rillet uses Vercel Connect to give its agents access to Slack and Linear through reusable connections the team can attach to the projects that need them. Connect supplies short-lived tokens at runtime and handles refresh through its SDK, keeping long-lived provider secrets out of each application and giving builders fewer credentials to maintain. If a runtime token leaks, its expiration limits how long it can be used.

Anthony's team built a Slack bot that picks up tickets and opens PRs, while others run agents for incident analysis and Linear board management. Shared conventions make that work easier to reuse, and agent building has spread beyond engineering.

Running customer requests through agents, end to end

Before, when a customer would ask for a change, and the request would scatter across a Linear ticket, a Slack thread, and a catch-up conversation with an engineer. By the time anyone had the full context, the fastest part of the job was writing the code.

The person closest to the customer ships the fix

Rillet's customer success team now opens a Chrome extension alongside the Rillet app, highlights what the customer is seeing, and describes the change. The extension's eve agent captures the context and, if the change is safe and well-scoped, hands it to a coding agent that writes the spec, makes the change, and opens a pull request assigned to Anthony. Agents also spin up a browser in a sandbox to test the change and attach screenshots as proof, while Anthony reviews the pull request and merges it. If he requests changes, the agent resumes its session and addresses them.

Rillet's CEO recently posted that the company shipped more in the past few weeks than in the entire first half of 2026, on top of tripling its shipping rate over the prior three months. Rillet’s CPA team ships customer requests through its in-house agent, Nebula, within two hours of the ask. As one of their customers put it, Rillet has "completely ruined my expectations" for how quickly software vendors should make changes.

Using AI Gateway to give every builder every model

As more people at Rillet started building agents, connecting directly to Anthropic and OpenAI meant configuring access to each model provider separately. AI Gateway routes model requests to both through one integration, so builders can add an agent without setting up separate provider connections.

The model is a string

In eve, builders choose the model by setting a string in the agent’s configuration:

Agents deployed on Vercel authenticate to AI Gateway automatically. Builders can try different models for a task by changing the model string, without changing the integration. Usage breakdowns show Anthony which models the team uses and what they cost, helping him track spending and choose models as more people build autonomous agents.

Managing builder access through Enterprise Managed Users

As more people are building agents, Rillet also needs to manage their access to Vercel. With Enterprise Managed Users, builders sign in through Google Workspace single sign-on using company-managed accounts rather than personal ones. Directory Sync adds and removes their access based on assignments in Rillet’s identity provider, so account administration follows the company’s directory.

Rillet set up Enterprise Managed Users on its own and moved builders from personal to company-managed accounts in one transition, bringing their Vercel sign-in and account access under Rillet’s identity provider.

What's next

Anthony is building what Rillet thinks of as its agent factory, so bigger features can follow the same pipeline as small fixes. One agent writes PRDs and technical specs, while another connects to Rillet's Linear boards, Miro diagrams, and knowledge base to give other agents the context they need. With subagents and delegation built into eve, Anthony can add these specialized agents as directories within the same framework.

For a company whose mission is collapsing month-long processes into zero days, building agents in eve and running them on Vercel brings that same focus on speed to its internal tooling.

About Rillet: Rillet is the AI-native ERP built for the era of agentic finance. By combining a real-time general ledger, continuous close architecture, and AI agents in one system, Rillet enables humans and agents to run finance together with full context, controls, and auditability.

title: AI Gateway adds confidence-based decision fallbacks
summary:
AI Gateway can now escalate a decision request to a fallback model when the primary model's answer trips a confidence condition you set.

Conditions can be combined, so an escalation can depend on more than one signal. The plain model names you already list in models keep catching outright errors, so existing fallbacks are unaffected. Confidence conditions cover Choice and Score questions. Boolean questions escalate on a probability range instead.

Set the fallback by adding one conditional object to providerOptions.gateway.models. Requests without it keep their existing behavior.

Leave out question and the condition checks every question of the matching type, so { confidenceBelow: 0.6 } escalates when any Choice or Score answer falls below 0.6.

Because a triggered fallback runs a second decision, it bills both stages.

Learn more in the decision fallbacks documentation, or see them in practice for mapping CSV columns and flagging UI copy for translation review.

title: Jev for Python engineers
summary:
It's simply impossible to not hear about Jev. Seemingly everyone is tinkering with it in some way, from using it to make trading decisions (what could possibly go wrong?) to generating UIs with it (maybe we're onto something here!).

Jev is a new kind of AI model. You feed it data and ask it a set of multiple-choice questions, and it responds with its answers and how confident it is in each. Just like with any other model, Jev can and will make mistakes, but it will make them fast. ​

​The bottom line is: Jev is built for making narrow decisions. Whether it's accurate enough for your use cases is something you'll need to test.

The job of the Python team at Vercel is to make it easy for Python devs to tinker with Jev, among a few other things. So please welcome the latest release of the AI SDK for Python.

Install it with uv add ai to use the new experimental evaluate() API, which talks directly to Jev's nervous system. Then create an AI Gateway key, set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, and try this complete example:

Now, I'd like to explain what Jev is and how to make it work for you using a couple of examples. One is good and one is dumb. Ask Jev which is which. Let's have some fun!

Jev ELI5

Jev is a universal classifier.

Classifiers are the classic primitive of good old machine learning. Say you want a spam filter. You train a classifier on lots of emails, each labeled as spam or not spam, and it learns to tell whether a freshly incoming email looks like spam.

Problem is, for every new classification task you'd have to collect and label new data, and then train a new classifier on it to tune its weights for that task. But you know what else has weights? Large language models! So the team behind Jev figured out how to turn an LLM into a classifier that you don't need to train for a specific domain, because it's already trained on a broad slice of human knowledge.

And while it started as an LLM, Jev still behaves like a classifier. It's cheap and fast, and it returns structured JSON instead of generating text. Its answers conform to the types and choices you define in your questions.

The API

Jev's official API couldn't be simpler, and to keep it that way, we implemented it in the Python AI SDK pretty much verbatim.

There's just one function, evaluate(), and a few supporting types. The function takes a model, state (can be a simple string or complex JSON), and a mapping of questions. A question is an instance of either ChoiceQuestion (choose one answer), ScoreQuestion (rate the state on a scale you define), or NoulQuestion (estimate the probability that a statement is true).

For the complete API reference, refer your agent to the docs. By now, we should have a good idea of what Jev is and how to use it. Time to see what we can build with it!

Example 1: Python or English?

This is a sensible example of using Jev: quite literally as a classifier.

About a year ago I had an idea to make the Python REPL agentic. I wanted it to have a great UX and thought it would be pretty cool if the REPL could tell whether I'm typing English or Python without me explicitly switching between chat and code.

I needed a classifier, so I spent two days training my own on a random selection of Python code and English text.

After a lot of sweat and dumb Opus 4.1 tokens, I concluded I'm not good enough to make a reliable classifier for Python vs. English. The UI felt jittery: typing if i highlighted it as Python, if i i switched it to English, and if i is flipped it back to Python. What seemed like a very simple problem turned out to be a really hard one.

Let's see how Jev does:

These are actual traces of Jev responses to "does this look like English or Python to you?" The code behind them isn't particularly interesting; it's basically the opening code snippet of this post with a different question.

What's more interesting is whether Jev could solve my REPL problem. And while it does seem to fare much better than my hand-rolled classifier did, it still has gaps. For example, "what's" + " up looks like English to Jev, while it's quite obvious to me that it's a partially typed Python expression.

Example 2: Jev writes Python code

How about we regress and make Jev generate text like an LLM? Jev can't write, so one way to get it to type is to have it go letter by letter. At each step, it picks the next character from a set of letters, punctuation, and whitespace. Another way would be to pick one word at a time from a vocabulary of some N English words.

When I saw that, I immediately knew I had to test how good Jev is at writing Python code.

My first attempt used the "letters + Python keywords + whitespace" method, but I quickly realized Jev could barely type an if statement that way. The only way to get anything sensible out of it was to make it generate an abstract syntax tree (AST) of the program instead.

The idea:

  1. Take the user's prompt and use an LLM (GPT-5.6 in this case) to expand it into a concrete set of instructions for Jev. I found that without a detailed "plan", Jev struggles to implement even elementary tasks.

  2. Make Jev build a Python AST through a series of choices. At each step, show it the current program, mark the field being filled, and offer the possible next nodes, like a function call, an arithmetic operation, or a variable. Each option comes with a preview of the code it would produce.

  3. Apply each choice to the tree and render it back into Python. The host code handles punctuation and indentation; Jev decides the program's overall structure and contents. Repeat until Jev finishes the tree.

I did get Jev to generate syntactically valid (yet still mostly incorrect) Python code using this approach. But as you can see, making classifiers do the job of an LLM is quite challenging. The source code is on GitHub if you think you can do better.

Try Jev

Neither experiment worked quite as I'd hoped, but I'm still excited about Jev. We're only beginning to explore what this new class of models can do!

Try it today with the AI SDK for Python and let us know what you build. All you need is uv add ai and an AI Gateway key. Here's a ready to copy/paste prompt for your coding agent:
